However, the gate test: a reader who has followed the draft knows Perth as the blacksmith from the harpoon-tempering scene (Ch 113 in the source, not on the removal list). I will treat this as established in prior surviving draft chapters and not flag it.

**"the life-buoy-coffin still lightly swung"** — the draft opens Ch 134 with "the life-buoy-coffin still lightly swung." Does the preceding draft chapter (Ch 132) establish a life-buoy-coffin? Ch 132 is the cabin scene; it contains no reference to a life-buoy-coffin. The source of Ch 132 also contains no such reference. The life-buoy-coffin is introduced in Ch 126 of the source (Ahab converts Queequeg's coffin into a life-buoy). Whether that chapter survived compression matters. Ch 126 is not on the authorized-removal list, so it should appear in the draft sequence. The *immediately preceding* draft chapter shown is Ch 132, but Ch 134 comes after Ch 132 in the source numbering — Ch 133 ("The Chase — First Day") would intervene. The task says "consecutive chapters" as presented. Here Ch 132 and Ch 134 are the pair shown; Ch 133 is not shown. This is not a mid-scene jump introduced by the immediately preceding chapter — the object was set up chapters earlier and the "still" is continuity language. Not a finding.

**"the shattered, white ribs and splintered planks"** — the source says "shears, which, in some whaling-ships, cross the quarter-deck… serving to carry the spare, unrigged, or disabled boats" and "Upon the stranger's shears were beheld the shattered, white ribs…" The draft says "Upon her shears were beheld the shattered, white ribs…" cutting the gloss on what "shears" are. Is this a missing definitional gloss (test 4)? A competent reader might not know what "shears" are in the whaling-ship context. The draft uses "her shears" without any identifier. This could leave the reader unable to place what "shears" refers to on the ship.

Gate test: a reader with no source access reads "Upon her shears were beheld the shattered, white ribs and splintered planks of what had once been a whale-boat." Without the gloss, "shears" is an undefined shipboard term. The reader cannot confidently picture where on the ship this wreckage is displayed, though they do understand wreckage of a whale-boat exists. This is mild but the term "shears" is genuinely opaque without the gloss — it is not recoverable from context alone (unlike, say, "the helm" or "the deck"). This meets test 4.
